On Wed, 22 Oct 2003 09:53:00 +0100 (BST), Steve Buckland wrote
> > OK - I had forgotten what the options were. So the problem is simply
> > insufficient replication to use that approach. Yes, use of t with
> > 1df widens the ci enormously - but so it should, if you treat the
> > strata as replicates - note that the CVs of the combined estimates
> > are much too small, and are badly estimated because of the lack of
> > replication. The huge t value counteracts this.

Well thank you Steve and Len!, it does have sense

However, if there are
> > good estimates of variance for the 2 separate estimates, then of
> > course we can do much better for estimating precision on mean
> > density across seasons. e.g. if D=(D1+D2)/2
> >
> > var(D) = (var(D1)+var(D2))/4 then get the ci based on this variance.


Ok, but when you said var(D), do you mean the statisitc variance of the mean
density? Im asking because Distance give my only the Standard Error of the
strata densities, and should I consider var(D)=SE^2 (because of Var=S^2)?
or var(D)=SE?
Furthermore, when I had my new var of global density [var(D)], as you
explained, should I get the CI by a Z or t distribution?


> >
> > It is easy to extend this for a weighted average. To be honest, I
> > had assumed that Distance would be based on this approach when
> > weighting is by effort, though I can see either approach can be
> > useful, depending on circumstances. Is there a reason that Distance
> > doesn't incorporate this approach?
